text: The interesting part of garment engineering is that the load paths are dynamic. A strap is a suspension system, and the materials science that goes into the elastic recovery is closer to what you would find in an aerospace lab than a fashion house. Sizing is the unsolved problem: bodies vary along more axes than any sizing chart admits, which is why the return rates are so high. The closest consumer analogue is probably running shoes, where fit also dominates satisfaction, but even there the variation is lower.

text: Wood is a much better structural material than people give it credit for. Laminated bamboo has a strength to weight ratio that competes with mid grade aluminium, damps vibration better than carbon, and fails slowly and visibly instead of catastrophically. The reason it never took over cycling is manufacturing consistency: every stalk is different, so every frame needs individual validation, and that does not scale. The industry optimised for repeatability instead, the same way running shoes converged on injection moulded EVA rather than anything bespoke. Repeatability wins markets even when the bespoke option is better for any individual buyer, because the warranty math only works when units are interchangeable. You see the same dynamic in furniture, in framing lumber grades, and in the difference between a luthier's instrument and a factory guitar. The market does not reward the best object, it rewards the most predictable one, and wood is gloriously, fatally unpredictable.
